articles.title_orig: US signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months, committee says
articles.title_zh: US signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months, committee says
articles.content_orig:
The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. As of May, there had been 3.4 million requested sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices .
"Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents.
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks continued.
The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China.
In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries.
Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS —  Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions.
"Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting.

articles.title_orig: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
articles.title_zh: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
articles.content_orig:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake
Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump , California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway .
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.
Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep . Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News .
Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health , often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: U.N. Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: U.N. Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.content_orig:
Rohingya genocide: What was said in court and what happens now?
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.
Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
Rohingyas at the Cox's Bazar camp in Bangladesh, where around a million refugees now reside, watched the verdict live
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.
After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.
Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.
The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
Watch: Genocide judgement will 'mean a great deal' for Rohingya community
Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.
He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.
Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.
While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.
Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.
In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.
The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.
It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.
The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."
Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".
Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".
To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.
Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.
Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest of crimes under international law.
Rohingya refugees were seen reacting as the ICJ verdict was broadcast on a big screen in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh
Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".
He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.
However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.
The ruling will, though, have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.
Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings.
He added that, while ruling against Myanmar did not mean the court would find similarly with Gaza, if it had not found Myanmar responsible, the case against Israel "would, in effect, be over". Israel says the case against it is "wholly unfounded".
ICJ president Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population
Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, told the BBC that the court had not accepted Myanmar's counter-terrorism defence and had found for the first time that rape and sexual violence was an act of genocide, positions it would bear in mind for future cases.
A spokesperson for the US State Department said "the proper interpretation" of the Genocide Convention is of "paramount importance", and so is "preventing politicisation" of the International Criminal Court. "We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," they said.
They said they share the "grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups", and added the US is the "leading donor for the Rohingya refugee humanitarian response".
Following Thursday's ruling, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the government was ordering Myanmar's defence attachÃ© be expelled and that he was summoning its charge d'affaires.
He pledged to set out "further action in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held to account" after a cross-party group of MPs called for the government to resume sanctions against Myanmar's military.

articles.title_orig: What the Blue Wave in Texas Means for Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX
articles.title_zh: What the Blue Wave in Texas Means for Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX
articles.content_orig:
On Valentine’s Day in 2024, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott interrupted a private dinner with his wife to take a call from Elon Musk.
Mr. Musk had recently been rebuked by a court in Delaware, where his two largest companies, SpaceX and Tesla, were incorporated. A judge had voided Mr. Musk’s pay package at Tesla, valued at about $50 billion, calling it “an unfathomable sum.”
Mr. Musk had spent years building a close relationship with the Republican governor. Now, on the call, Mr. Musk wanted to know if Mr. Abbott would support Mr. Musk’s businesses if he incorporated them in Texas, rather than Delaware.
“One hundred percent,” Mr. Abbott said, recounting the story in a 2025 speech at the University of Texas School of Law.
Mr. Musk followed through, further entwining his trillion-dollar electric vehicle maker, Tesla, and his two-trillion-dollar rocket maker, SpaceX, with the state. Mr. Musk had been cultivating Texas’s Republican leaders since he moved there in 2020. For a while, the strategy paid off handsomely. Mr. Abbott held up his end of the Valentine’s Day bargain, awarding Mr. Musk and his businesses at least $1.7 billion in grants, tax breaks and other incentives in the past two years, according to a New York Times analysis.
Since this month’s election , Mr. Musk’s big bet on Texas has become vulnerable. Texans voted out many of his political allies, including Mr. Abbott , even after Mr. Musk gave Republicans nearly $500 million nationwide.

Ukraine's military said it struck "one of the largest oil refineries in southern Russia" in the lead-up to President Donald Trump's meeting Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump will meet one-on-one with Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, China, a U.S. official confirmed to Fox News on Wednesday.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said explosions "rocked" Russia's Krasnodar Krai region last night and into this morning as Ukrainian forces "carried out air strikes against the Ilsky and Afipsky oil refineries, two key fuel suppliers in southern Russia."

"Located in southern Russia, they provide some of the shortest supply routes for delivering fuel to Russian forces deployed on the frontline," it also said about the two facilities. "Consequently, every fire at these facilities means less diesel and petrol for the Russian military, and fewer oil revenues for the Russian aggressor to purchase missiles and Shahed-type attack drones."

articles.title_orig: AMD shares slide as report says China links could invite US scrutiny
articles.title_zh: AMD shares slide as report says China links could invite US scrutiny
articles.content_orig:
Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices were down about 7% Wednesday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."
Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.
The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."
The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.
"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."
Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Trump, Xi and Putin Seek to Project Power at Their First Summit
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Trump, Xi and Putin Seek to Project Power at Their First Summit
articles.content_orig:
It was the first-ever meeting of the leaders of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers—one that host Xi Jinping opened by hailing its “pioneering significance.”
Exactly what was achieved when Xi met with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump at Kylin Villa in northwestern Shenzhen on Thursday, however, has onlookers scratching their heads. Xi started by invoking the responsibility of Great Powers toward world peace; Putin delved into historic “shared interests;” while Trump immediately lashed out at “rogue globalist organisations,” such as the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The ICC “has gotten out of control,” Trump told his companions seated around a round wooden table, and has “really strayed far beyond its jurisdiction.”
It was almost as if this historic trilateral , held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, didn’t have any fixed agenda. It hadn’t. When the confab was first proposed, Putin wanted to talk about Ukraine, though U.S. officials pushed back. Trump instead suggested nuclear arms and Iran, but Beijing wasn’t keen. Finally, China’s Foreign Ministry settled on “safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations.”
It was therefore an occasion rich with platitudes but not a lot else. “In this global village, major countries shoulder special responsibilities,” said Xi, who also called for the destruction of all nuclear weapons. “Positive interaction among major powers is not an optional question, but a compulsory one.”
Still, the meeting served its purpose. Trump gained a chance to project influence after chastening midterms and the unfolding Nvidia saga that forced the resignation of his close friend Jensen Huang as CEO. Xi got to flaunt himself as the consummate statesman, while Putin took a baby step out from the diplomatic cold. But it was also a distinctly unsettling sight for the U.S. President to be sitting beside two of America’s most consequential adversaries, whose governments declared in 2022 that their friendship with each other had “no limits.”
Before the three-way meeting, Trump met separately with Putin and then Xi. His roughly 40 minutes with the Russian President began on a hopeful note: “Wonderful things can come out of this—or at least start,” Trump said. During an hour of talks with Xi, Trump returned to a more familiar concern. “I’ll be asking you to do some more for our farmers,” he said. He also suggested that Washington and Beijing could work together to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.
That prospect mattered to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said Wednesday that the war could end in a single meeting if the U.S. and China used their economic leverage against Moscow. Instead, Trump launched a broadside against the ICC, which has issued an arrest warrant against Putin for war crimes, urging his autocratic counterparts to cooperate on “ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty.”
Trump also said it was “vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world,” before segueing into a justification of his war in Iran : “That’s what we’re doing in Iran. We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Of course, this was always going to be an occasion that would put style over substance. On Wednesday, Xi surprised onlookers by greeting a clearly delighted Trump on the tarmac at Shenzhen Baoan Airport. Their handshake turned into a brief hug, before five People’s Liberation Army J-10C fighter jets flew overhead, billowing red, yellow, and blue smoke.
In personally meeting Trump as he deplaned Air Force One, Xi reciprocated the welcome he received from the U.S. President at Joint Base Andrews in September. The gesture was a first by a top Chinese leader since Mao Zedong met Nikita Khrushchev at Beijing’s airport in 1959.
Putin had to suffice with being greeted by Xi’s chief of staff, Cai Qi, upon his earlier arrival in the wee hours of Wednesday morning. But Xi spent much of that afternoon in talks with his embattled Russian counterpart, who used his speech to assembled CEOs to lambast Western sanctions, crowing that the U.S. and Europe had “punished themselves” with punitive measures, which Russia had successfully sidestepped anyway.
Upon emerging from his two-hour bilateral with Putin, Xi called on both countries to “lead and advance … the democratization of international relations.” Putin, in turn, boasted that economic coercion was “a thing of the past.” Later in the evening, Putin and Trump shook hands before the gala dinner as Xi looked on smiling.
“Beijing’s top priority would be to create a more stable external environment for China’s development, particularly by making relations with Washington more predictable while maintaining steady cooperation with Moscow,” says Sun Chenghao, a fellow with Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy.
Still, the summit threatened to be overshadowed by the Nvidia scandal, with company founder Huang admitting an affair with a woman accused of illicitly funneling chips to China and whom U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly suspect may be a Chinese spy. On Nov. 16, the U.S. Commerce Department issued an interim rule aimed at stopping Chinese firms from accessing advanced U.S. chips through data centers abroad.
Trump told Fox News that he and Xi “spoke the whole evening” during Wednesday’s gala dinner but only “briefly” discussed Nvidia. Trump also claimed he was unaware of the espionage allegations, which China vehemently denies. “I haven’t heard that she was a spy,” Trump said. “She was a businesswoman who bought chips, and who knows if they were bought right or wrong.”
Trump also appeared to shoot down any hopes of regulation governing AI: “We oppose any form of globalist regulation or anything to control or stifle [AI], and we won’t allow that to happen,” he said.
Still, the historic trilateral did succeed in visibly placing China at the center of Great Power diplomacy. Hosting the leaders alongside APEC supports Beijing’s claim that global influence is shifting eastward, with China as a stabilizing power, particularly amid unpredictable U.S. policy.
“The optics might actually play well for China,” says Chong Ja Ian, a professor of international relations at the National University of Singapore. “It certainly would fit the sort of image that Beijing and Xi would like to create for themselves.”
But while APEC was created in 1989 to ease trade and investment across the region, today’s world has been gripped by rising protectionism. The Trump Administration has levied tariffs on 60 trading partners that together account for 99.4% of U.S. imports, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. Moreover, Europe is increasingly chary about cheap Chinese exports that Brussels says are fueled by subsidies and industrial overcapacity.
Xi used his Wednesday address to business leaders to promise a more open Chinese market and present the world’s second-largest economy as a source of opportunity. “History tells us that opening doors brings progress while closing doors leaves one behind,” he said.
Yet the image of three elderly leaders debating global problems behind closed doors sits uneasily beside Xi’s call for a more multipolar world. Pro-Kremlin media was especially keen to frame the meeting as Yalta 2.0 after the historic powwow between Roosevelt, Stalin, and Churchill toward the end of World War II.
But it is Ukraine’s plucky defiance of that invasion that underscores how today’s Middle Powers have more agency. At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney urged third countries to work together on trade, security and technology in order to shape the rules and resist economic coercion. “Middle powers must act together because if you are not at the table, you are on the menu,” Carney said.

articles.title_orig: US mortgage rates rise for the first time in five weeks | CNN Business
articles.title_zh: US mortgage rates rise for the first time in five weeks | CNN Business
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates are climbing again after a few weeks of easing following a three-year high.
The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 7.28% this week, up from 7.11% last week, according to Freddie Mac. It’s the largest one-week jump since the week of October 1.
That’s also more than a full percentage point jump compared to this time last year, when the average was 6.26%.
Mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury yield, which moved higher recently after a hotter-than-expected inflation report increased the odds that the Federal Reserve could hike its benchmark interest rate at its December policy meeting.
Mortgage rates have now stayed stubbornly over 7% since late September – the highest they’ve been at any time since 2000 – aside from a single month in 2023.
That has further pumped the brakes on an already stalled housing market. Pending home sales, which measures home transactions that haven’t officially closed yet, collapsed in October to a record low, according to a report released by the National Association of Realtors on Wednesday. Pending deals fell 4.7% between September and October, and nearly 17% year-over-year.
“It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million,” said Lawrence Yun, NAR’s chief economist, in a statement. “Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.”

articles.title_orig: TSMC tightens China AI chip curbs as new US rules close manufacturing loophole, sources say
articles.title_zh: TSMC tightens China AI chip curbs as new US rules close manufacturing loophole, sources say
articles.content_orig:
The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. As of May, there had been 3.4 million requested sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices .
"Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents.
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks continued.
The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China.
In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries.
Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS —  Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions.
"Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting.
This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates.
— Megan Cassella contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump says US will 'see what happens' in conflict with Iran after January 1
articles.title_zh: Trump says US will 'see what happens' in conflict with Iran after January 1
articles.content_orig:
Iran's foreign ministry rejected President Trump's accusations the country is developing chemical or biological weapons and compared the situation to then-Secretary of State Colin Powell asserting Iraq had weapons of mass destruction.
"After the grand narrative of the 'Iranian nuclear threat,' U.S. officials are now claiming that there are indications Iran is developing biological or chemical weapons!" Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X . "The allegations keep changing, but the underlying narrative remains disturbingly familiar. Once again, the world is apparently expected to suffer a bout of collective amnesia."
Baqaei raised the specter of the U.S. invasion of Iraq in 2003 over alleged development of weapons of mass destruction by Saddam Hussein's government and asked why Americans would fall for it again.
"Do American officials really expect the world to forget Colin Powell's infamous appearance before the U.N. Security Council in 2003, when he held up a small vial as a visual representation of the alleged threat posed by Iraq's weapons of mass destruction?" the spokesperson said. "That moment has since become an enduring symbol of one of the most consequential intelligence failures and political deceptions in modern history."
He added, "And now we find ourselves facing ominous new allegations and a narrative that appears to be following the same fraudulent script."
Mr. Trump on Wednesday had claimed there was an "indication" Iran was looking to develop chemical or biological weapons because the U.S. had "shut them out" of obtaining nuclear weapons.
"They're looking at gases, looking at bio, because we've shut them out with the nuclear," Mr. Trump told a Fox reporter in Shenzhen, China.
The Senate rejected a House-adopted resolution aimed at reining in President Trump's ability to strike Iran, losing Republican support despite frustration with the war following the party's losses in the midterm elections.
In a 48 to 51 vote, three Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky — joined all but one Senate Democrat — Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania — in support of the measure.
Thursday's vote marked the first time either chamber has weighed in on the war since the midterm elections, which dealt Republicans sweeping losses. Voters cited the war in Iran, and its toll on the economy, as among their top concerns.
The resolution would have directed the president "to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran," but its impact would have been largely symbolic.
Iraqi forces will begin deploying on Friday in the main stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah group, state media reported, as Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi steps up efforts to rein in the faction.
Kataeb Hezbollah on Tuesday adopted a softer tone toward the U.S.-backed premier, with Iraqi sources saying a compromise was reached during a visit by Iranian commander Esmail Qaani.
Iraq has faced mounting U.S. pressure to curb Iran's influence and contain Tehran-backed armed groups — a difficult task in a country long caught between its two allies.

"I'm not rushing to make any decisions on Iran," Mr. Trump told Keshet 12's Barak Ravid, who spoke to the president as he returned from China. "We'll see what happens after the new year starts."
The story noted Mr. Trump could also change his mind, though.
The tone seems in line with his and Secretary of State Marco Rubio's comments from last week. Mr. Trump called new strikes "quite unlikely," while Rubio said new strikes weren't needed since the economic sanctions campaign was working so well.
In an interview with Fox News on Wednesday, Mr. Trump said he had no need to ask China or Russia for help with an Iran deal.
"They want to make a deal, so I don't need help," Mr. Trump told the network. "I mean, I'm not going to go in asking for help. And frankly, they've treated us very well. They haven't fired. They haven't put ships in the water."

"That number includes munitions, equipment replacement costs, and operational cost," Arthur Miller, the Pentagon's deputy comptroller, told lawmakers during a hearing on his nomination as assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management.
The figure does not include damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East, some of which have been hit hard by Iranian drone and missile attacks, nor does it take into account the harm to the global economy.

The bulk of that price tag at the time was replacing used munitions at about $29 billion. Lost equipment, including planes and unmanned aircraft, accounted for about $6 billion.

"We do not accept being targeted on the one hand and being asked in a demanding tone on the other to provide accurate information about our materials and facilities and to provide unlimited access to them," Reza Najafi, Iran's ambassador and permanent representative to the United Nations and international organizations in Vienna, said Thursday, according to Iran's semi-official ISNA news agency.
"While adhering to its obligations, Iran will not accept unconditional and unlimited cooperation with the Agency [IAEA] and will review each inspection request on a case-by-case basis, taking into account security conditions," he added.
The nuclear issue, including IAEA access to Iran's nuclear sites, has been a key sticking point in negotiations between Tehran and Washington.
President Trump has justified the war as a necessary action to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Iran has always denied any nuclear weapons aspirations, but it has enriched uranium to near-weapons grade. The exact whereabouts and condition of that material, and the circumstances of many facilities themselves, have remained unclear since the U.S. and Israel launched a major attack on the sites in June 2025. Iran has refused IAEA access to its nuclear facilities since then.
Saudi Arabia has condemned Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen for targeting a skyscraper in the financial district of Riyadh, the kingdom's capital.

Earlier, Saudi Arabia's civil defense agency said the building was damaged in a Houthi strike but that there were no injuries.

articles.title_orig: From tarmac to APEC summit table, Japan's PM cuts a lonely figure
articles.title_zh: From tarmac to APEC summit table, Japan's PM cuts a lonely figure
articles.content_orig:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a subdued welcome on her first trip to China as premier, signaling Beijing's limited appetite for repairing ties strained by a simmering row over Taiwan.
At gatherings such as this week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, protocol details — including who greets a visiting leader at the airport and where they are positioned in official photographs — often convey political messages.
Takaichi was met on the tarmac Wednesday by a retired Chinese diplomat, rather than a serving official, and Japan's ambassador to China, Kenji Kanasugi.
The low-key reception contrasted sharply with the warmer welcomes given to other visiting leaders, including South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, while U.S. President Donald Trump was greeted personally by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
In the leaders' group photo, Takaichi was placed in the back row, off to the side and several places from Xi, who stood alongside Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Beijing sought to downgrade her official status to that of a head of government rather than a head of state," said Jeremy Chan, senior analyst at Eurasia Group.
During Thursday morning's greeting line, Takaichi spent several minutes trying to talk to the Chinese leader without an interpreter present, while most leaders exchanged handshakes and kept walking.
"It has become increasingly difficult for her to engage in formal or even informal conversations with Xi," said Kei Koga, an associate professor at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, who sees Takaichi's intention as to still "project the image that she could still communicate with him despite the ongoing tensions."
At a press briefing Thursday afternoon, Takaichi said Japan's position on Taiwan remained unchanged as stated in the 1972 Japan-China Communique, adding that her leadership has been communicating with Chinese counterparts on rare earth export controls.
Takaichi's subdued reception signaled Beijing's lack of enthusiasm to repair ties with Tokyo, analysts said, potentially prolonging China's curbs on critical mineral exports that have gripped Japanese industries for the past year.
"China's frosty reception of Takaichi shows quite clearly that Beijing is not yet ready to forgive her over her remarks about Taiwan," Chan said, expecting the bilateral relationship to remain strained until Takaichi leaves office.
That could leave Japan grappling with continued restrictions on rare earth supplies from China next year, said Tianchen Xu, senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit.
Relations deteriorated sharply after Takaichi said in November 2025 that a Taiwan Strait crisis could constitute a situation threatening Japan's survival and warrant a self-defense response.
While the substance broadly aligned with Japan's existing security policy, previous prime ministers had generally avoided stating it so explicitly in a Taiwan scenario.
China reacted angrily and demanded that Takaichi retract the remarks. She has not done so, while stating that the door to dialogue with Beijing remains open, with minimal high-level contact over the past year.
China has since tightened restrictions affecting Japan, including controls on dual-use and rare earth exports with potential military uses. It also discouraged its citizens from traveling to Japan and halted Japanese seafood imports.
Takaichi's visit marked the first trip to China by a Japanese prime minister since Shinzo Abe traveled to Chengdu in December 2019 for a trilateral summit with Chinese and South Korean leaders.
No formal Takaichi-Xi meeting has been publicly scheduled during her visit. Meanwhile, Xi is expected to join Trump and Putin for a historic trilateral gathering on Thursday, alongside a bilateral meeting with Trump.
Takaichi needs to show a "reflection of what she said about Taiwan a year ago," said Huiyao Wang, founder of the Beijing-based Center for China and Globalization, which is often seen as close to Beijing's thinking.
Wang said Tokyo should show greater flexibility, pointing to Trump's comments that the U.S. would avoid getting involved in the Taiwan issue. He argued that Japan holding firm on the issue would not help relations with Beijing.
Such reflection, he said, "would really help to clarify some of those misunderstandings between the two countries."
— CNBC's Evelyn Cheng contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump calls Putin and Xi friends. They have other plans.
articles.title_zh: Trump calls Putin and Xi friends. They have other plans.
articles.content_orig:
President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin sat down together in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday in a rare face-to-face encounter for the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries, but there appeared to be little concrete to show for the meeting in terms of resolving any of the crises facing the world.
The leaders offered a joint statement after their roughly hour-and-a-half-long meeting. Mr. Trump immediately left for his return flight to the U.S. without speaking to journalists on the ground. On the flight home, the president said on social media he will hold a press conference at noon on Friday to discuss the trip.
The presidents discussed Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine , which Mr. Trump has wanted to bring to a negotiated end. But the only significant statement on the conflict came after the meeting from Putin, who ruled out any direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing a major strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces on a key bridge in Russian-held Crimea.
Putin's senior aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the meeting that the atmosphere had been good, and the Kremlin quickly released what it called a joint statement from all three leaders characterizing the talks. The White House later provided the same statement.
The three men "exchanged views in detail on the current international situation and reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the readout said, adding that as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, they had "reaffirmed their commitment to reforming the UN so that it can more effectively respond to global challenges and fulfill its fundamental mission in the area of international peace and security."
They also committed to increasing gas and oil production "for the benefit of all countries," agreed on the "fundamental importance" of "the principle of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials," and said the " International Criminal Court and other similar bodies should not abuse their powers."
Finally, the leaders "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war, and that it should never be unleashed."
The White House indicated that Mr. Trump might speak with reporters on Air Force One during the flight back to the U.S.
The Kremlin shared a short video on social media, via Russian state media, showing Xi accompanying Putin as they walked out of the meeting to Putin's waiting motorcade. Before they exit the building, Putin is seen shaking Xi's hand, thanking him for hosting the gathering and telling him, according to Russian state media, that nobody had expected it to go so well.
Before the meeting, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and then with Xi.
"We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said, standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."
As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend."
Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine, who sits on the Committee on Foreign Relations, said the image of Mr. Trump standing with Xi and Putin was concerning.
"Some of the pictures troubled me, seeing the president stand with Putin and Xi, rather than seeing the president stand with the leaders of the global democracies," Kaine said. "When I saw them, it turned my stomach a bit, and particularly President Trump's declaration that Vladimir Putin was a friend. Vladimir Putin is not a friend, and so you know he was either being insincere or he is deeply deluded if he thinks Vladimir Putin is a friend."
In a phone call with NBC reporter Gabe Gutierrez, Mr. Trump called the meeting a 12 on a scale of zero to 10.
Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic discussed by the two leaders, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood."
After the trilateral talks Thursday, Putin told reporters that Ukraine and Europe were "not yet ready" to make the compromises necessary to resolve the war, according to Russian media.
"We will not negotiate after the attacks on the Crimean bridge," he declared, referring to this week's Ukrainian strike on the highly symbolic Kerch Bridge, which links Russia with Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin said Kyiv and Europe would eventually come to understand that it is better to make compromises than to face "realities."
Ukraine and its European partners have long feared that the White House appears willing to offer Putin too much — including the prospect of major energy deals — with no significant concessions from Russia  in return, while putting pressure on Kyiv to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.
Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way meeting. As the Trump-Xi session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States were "stable and improved."
Mr. Trump told reporters he had spoken with Xi for two hours on Wednesday, with trade and tariffs being the main topics. He also said he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite."
Mr. Trump said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with his fellow leaders. Russia and the United States are by far the world's largest holders of nuclear weapons , with stockpiles estimated at well over 5,000 warheads, while China is believed to be a distant third, with about 600 weapons.
Putin has made denuclearization a key talking point for decades, but both he and Mr. Trump have allowed previous treaties intended to limit nuclear proliferation to lapse in recent years. China, which has been building up its nuclear program , ruled out taking part in any denuclearization talks with the U.S. and Russia as recently as last year .
China's state-run Xinhua news agency quoted Xi , however, as saying ahead of the trilateral meeting on Thursday that nuclear weapons were a "sword of Damocles hanging over humanity," and calling for them to be "completely banned and completely destroyed, leading to a world free of nuclear weapons."
The Kremlin said in its readout of the three-way meeting that it would "continue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons" with China and the U.S.
A range of other global challenges lingered in the background of the trilateral meeting, including the war in Iran and tension over trade and artificial intelligence .
The summit took place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang , whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed , is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing.
Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.

This week, Zaidi gave Kataeb Hezbollah a deadline to withdraw from Jurf al-Sakher, also known as Jurf al-Nasr, which lies south of Baghdad, after the government said an investigative committee had confirmed oil smuggling in the area — a claim the armed group denied.
President Trump told Channel 12 News in Israel that he is in no hurry to make any decisions on the war with Iran, and could in fact wait until next year.
"I'm not rushing to make any decisions on Iran," Mr. Trump told Keshet 12's Barak Ravid, who spoke to the president as he returned from China. "We'll see what happens after the new year starts."
The story noted Mr. Trump could also change his mind, though.
The tone seems in line with his and Secretary of State Marco Rubio's comments from last week. Mr. Trump called new strikes "quite unlikely," while Rubio said new strikes weren't needed since the economic sanctions campaign was working so well.
In an interview with Fox News on Wednesday, Mr. Trump said he had no need to ask China or Russia for help with an Iran deal.
"They want to make a deal, so I don't need help," Mr. Trump told the network. "I mean, I'm not going to go in asking for help. And frankly, they've treated us very well. They haven't fired. They haven't put ships in the water."
The war against Iran has cost the U.S. military more than $48 billion since the conflict began in late February, a Pentagon official said Thursday.
"That number includes munitions, equipment replacement costs, and operational cost," Arthur Miller, the Pentagon's deputy comptroller, told lawmakers during a hearing on his nomination as assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management.
The figure does not include damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East, some of which have been hit hard by Iranian drone and missile attacks, nor does it take into account the harm to the global economy.
The update was the first since mid-October, when the war's cost was pegged at $47.1 billion, according to an estimate from the U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News. The bulk of that price tag at the time was replacing used munitions at about $29 billion. Lost equipment, including planes and unmanned aircraft, accounted for about $6 billion.
Iran said Thursday that it will not accept "unconditional and unlimited cooperation" with inspectors from the United Nations' International Atomic Energy Agency while it is being bombed.
"We do not accept being targeted on the one hand and being asked in a demanding tone on the other to provide accurate information about our materials and facilities and to provide unlimited access to them," Reza Najafi, Iran's ambassador and permanent representative to the United Nations and international organizations in Vienna, said Thursday, according to Iran's semi-official ISNA news agency.
"While adhering to its obligations, Iran will not accept unconditional and unlimited cooperation with the Agency [IAEA] and will review each inspection request on a case-by-case basis, taking into account security conditions," he added.
The nuclear issue, including IAEA access to Iran's nuclear sites, has been a key sticking point in negotiations between Tehran and Washington.
President Trump has justified the war as a necessary action to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Iran has always denied any nuclear weapons aspirations, but it has enriched uranium to near-weapons grade. The exact whereabouts and condition of that material, and the circumstances of many facilities themselves, have remained unclear since the U.S. and Israel launched a major attack on the sites in June 2025. Iran has refused IAEA access to its nuclear facilities since then.
Saudi Arabia has condemned Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen for targeting a skyscraper in the financial district of Riyadh, the kingdom's capital.
"The Ministry of Foreign Affairs expresses the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's strong condemnation and denunciation of the continued terrorist attacks by the Houthi terrorist militia targeting civilian and economic facilities and civilian objects in the capital, Riyadh, and the resulting material damage to the King Abdullah Financial District," the ministry wrote in a post on X .
Earlier, Saudi Arabia's civil defense agency said the building was damaged in a Houthi strike but that there were no injuries.
The Iran-backed Houthis struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district on Thursday, causing damage but no injuries, Saudi authorities said.

articles.title_orig: UN could soon be leaderless as race to succeed Guterres stalls
articles.title_zh: UN could soon be leaderless as race to succeed Guterres stalls
articles.content_orig:
International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) chief Rafael Grossi is eyeing the position of United Nations secretary-general amid a tense race to replace Antonio Guterres.
The Argentinian nominee has finished second in the latest UN Security Council (UNSC) straw poll behind Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan , with nine “encourage” and four “discourage” votes and eight candidates still in the fray.
Grossi, 65, has earned admiration and criticism in equal measure for his IAEA tenure, defined by his hands-on approach to crisis diplomacy in active war zones, but also by accusations of partisanship, levelled against him, especially by Iran.
He is running on an agenda to reform the UN in a way seen as favourable to United States President Donald Trump and his political ally, Argentinian President Javier Milei.
But China and Russia – two of the five permanent UNSC members with veto power – are unlikely to back a candidate so closely aligned with Washington, analysts say, and a global civil society campaign is throwing its weight behind the selection of the first woman to lead the UN in the organisation’s 81-year history.
Grossi’s legacy at the IAEA and decades-long career as an Argentinian diplomat have cast him as a pragmatic crisis manager.
Since being appointed the UN nuclear watchdog’s director general in 2019, Grossi has been firmly in the front row in moments of international tension, including personally leading inspection teams to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Chornobyl nuclear power plants after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Jan Wouters, professor of international law and international organisations at KU Leuven in Belgium, said Grossi has “transformed the technical watchdog into a highly visible, proactive, diplomatic actor”.
“[He] significantly elevated the agency’s global profile through constant shuttle diplomacy and direct engagement with world leaders,” Wouters told Al Jazeera.
In Ukraine, by “focusing on technical safety rather than territorial sovereignty, he successfully brokered eight localised ceasefires between Russia and Ukraine to allow critical plant repairs” during the war, he added.
However, Ezequiel Jimenez Martinez, adjunct professor at the Pompeu Fabra law faculty in Barcelona, Spain, said Grossi’s very active role has “angered” the veto-wielding Russia, which sees him as having overstepped his position as agency head.
To be elected to lead the UN, a candidate needs at least nine votes in favour from the 15-member UNSC while avoiding a veto from any of its five permanent members (P5) – China, France, Russia, the US, and the United Kingdom. The 193-member UN General Assembly (UNGC) then has to sign off on the final choice.
The race is coming down to the wire, as Guterres must leave his post on December 31.
While none of the P5 has publicly announced its preference, the South China Morning Post reported that Beijing has ruled out Grossi for being too close to Washington and would instead back Grynspan.
While Iran is not a member of the UNSC, it has also been vocal in its opposition to Grossi as UN secretary-general. Tehran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, accused the IAEA this month of being overly influenced by the US and European countries in its “one-sided and biased reporting about Iran’s peaceful nuclear programme”.
The IAEA has estimated that Iran was holding 440.9kg (972lb) of uranium enriched to up to 60 percent before the June 2025 Israeli-US attacks on Iran’s nuclear facilities. While uranium must be enriched to 90 percent to become weapons-grade, the process becomes quick at 60 percent. The amount Tehran has would be enough, if enriched further, to build 10 nuclear weapons, according to the agency.
Jimenez Martinez said Grossi is likely to withstand the criticism, “because the majority of governors of the [IAEA] agree with his approach on Iran”.
“In the context of the UN, probably [this will lead to] a bit of fireworks, but I don’t think it will change many votes,” he said.
Grossi’s technical ability to lead the UN alone is unlikely to put him much ahead in the race, observers said. Candidates for the post of secretary-general must also be seen as defenders of the UN Charter and the UN’s international law and human rights instruments.
For this reason, support from the Argentinian president is seen as Grossi’s main liability. Milei has framed international institutions as threats to national sovereignty and individual liberty, describing the UN itself as “useless” and its diplomats as “fatally arrogant parasites”.
Since being elected president in 2023, Milei has reignited a longstanding dispute with the UK over the Falkland Islands , a British-administered territory over which Argentina claims sovereignty. Milei has told UN delegates that the principle of self-determination should not apply to the population of the islands, which Argentina calls Las Malvinas.
The Trump administration has also been a fierce critic of the UN, withdrawing Washington from key agencies, slashing UN funding and bypassing the body when it came to launching the war on Iran in February.
Jimenez Martinez said Grossi is seen as close to both Milei and Trump and as someone who could usher in a UN agenda aligned with their foreign policies.
“This will mean, in practice, a shrinking of the UN structure,” Jimenez Martinez said, including merging agencies and reorienting the body around security rather than development.
Grossi has called on world leaders to have the “courage to reform” the institution and lead it into a new era. According to Jimenez Martinez, his insistence on cutting red tape while failing to elaborate on safeguards is unlikely to get him a green light from the UNGA.
Alvina Hoffmann, senior lecturer in diplomatic studies at SOAS University of London, said Grossi is widely seen as a candidate whose “emphasis is on improving the system and cutting overlapping mandates, rather than addressing the structural drivers of inequality”.
He is also seen as someone who focuses on personal leadership, confidential negotiations and preventive diplomacy, “rather than issuing public declarations or condemnations”, which “might come at the expense of being able to call out violations of international law at a time in which international law is increasingly under attack”, Hoffmann said.
According to the tradition of geographical rotation, the UN secretary-general post should next go to a Latin American. Five women are running in the race, and public and civil society pressure is at an all-time high to elect the first woman to the post.
Grynspan ticks both boxes.
Ben Donaldson, adviser to the 1 for 8 Billion campaign, a civil society movement advocating for the appointment of the first female secretary-general, said that while electing the next UN chief should be based on merit, this criterion “is not inconsistent with gender considerations”.
UNGA “resolutions and international standards affirm that due regard should be given to achieving gender balance in senior UN leadership”, Donaldson told Al Jazeera.
“In applying these principles, member states should assess candidates not only on their individual competencies and experience, but also on how their personal characteristics and professional trajectories contribute to a leadership that reflects the diversity of the international community.”
“The United Nations has existed for 80 years without ever appointing a woman as secretary-general,” he added. “This persistent imbalance stands in contrast to the organisation’s own commitments to equality, parity and nondiscrimination.”

articles.title_orig: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you
articles.title_zh: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you
articles.content_orig:
Google on Thursday announced that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps, and browsing websites in the background.
The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other leading AI model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already been offering agentic features in their desktop applications for some time. Meanwhile, Google only this week announced the broader rollout of Gemini’s “Tasks,” the in-app feature that allows the AI to work more as an agent, helping users sign into websites, make online purchases, or book appointments.
Google also only recently began admitting early testers to try its revamped “CC” AI agent, announced in September , which is designed to help families stay organized across email, calendars, chats, and tasks.
Computer use is another type of agentic offering that allows an AI agent to take actions directly on the user’s computer — in Gemini’s case, a Mac. This allows the AI to complete multistep tasks that involve getting things done across local files, apps, and the web. After the user instructs the AI what they want to do, they’ll see the agent working in a live preview in their chat, while still keeping their screen and cursor free to continue working on other things.
As with other AI agents offering computer use, users can pause, stop, and approve Gemini’s actions before they happen.
Google suggests the feature could be useful for tedious tasks and other workflows, like filling out forms, repeating the same task over and over across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, creating slideshows from files or information in online dashboards, and more.
The feature is initially available in English in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. The company didn’t say when it would expand to other markets or platforms.

Google announced developer verification and changes to app sideloading last year. These changes started rolling out in four countries back in September, and the search giant has now announced a date for a global expansion.
Google has confirmed a January 2027 global rollout for these new developer rules and sideloading changes:
The company added that millions of apps have been registered around the world since verification kicked off in March, purportedly representing “over 99%” of all Android app installs.
For the uninitiated, Google requires app developers to verify their identity. Unverified apps can still be sideloaded on Android devices, but Google has also made enabling sideloading more difficult in the stated name of security and thwarting scammers.
Enabling sideloading on a device will entail a pretty lengthy process:
It’s worth noting that this change isn’t restricted to recent versions of Android, as it applies to devices running Android 7.0 or newer. Either way, it looks like sideloading is about to become more annoying for Android users globally.

articles.title_orig: AMD Slides After Hunterbrook Shorts Stock, Cites Circular Deals
articles.title_zh: AMD Slides After Hunterbrook Shorts Stock, Cites Circular Deals
articles.content_orig:
Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices were down about 7% Wednesday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."
Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.
The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."
The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.
"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."
Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.

articles.title_orig: Trump bought Nvidia, Palantir, SpaceX in September as federal deals, White House ties grew
articles.title_zh: Trump bought Nvidia, Palantir, SpaceX in September as federal deals, White House ties grew
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump's investment accounts bought shares of Nvidia , Palantir and Elon Musk 's SpaceX in September, around the time the companies secured major federal contracts and their executives met with the president, according to a newly released financial disclosure.
The 25-page filing shows 751 purchases and sales totaling between roughly $40.9 million and $148.1 million, according to a CNBC analysis. Purchases accounted for at least $29.2 million and sales at least $11.7 million. The filing reports transactions in broad dollar ranges, leaving the exact amounts and value of Trump's holdings unclear.
Among the transactions were Palantir purchases before the company received two federal contracts worth $42.5 million combined, according to contracting records, SpaceX investments shortly before and after a $946 million NASA contract expansion , and Nvidia trades as its then-CEO, Jensen Huang , cultivated a close relationship with Trump .
The trades underscore a striking feature of Trump's presidency: His personal fortune remains invested in companies whose fortunes his administration can shape. His accounts reported more than 21,000 trades in 2025 , compared with roughly 500 during his entire first term. Recent presidents have generally divested individual stocks or used blind trusts to avoid potential conflicts.
The White House has told CNBC previously Trump and his family have no control over the trades, which outside financial managers handle independently . The Trump Organization says the arrangement is designed to avoid even the appearance of a conflict. There is no evidence Trump directed the transactions or that his managers knew government decisions in advance.
White House spokesman Davis Ingle said that Trump's portfolio is independently managed and that neither the president nor his family has any input on trades. "All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers," Ingle told CNBC.
The Trump Organization did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The timing was particularly notable at Palantir, the artificial intelligence software maker whose technology is used by U.S. military, intelligence and civilian agencies.
Trump's accounts bought between $15,001 and $50,000 in Palantir shares on Sept. 2, followed by another purchase of between $1,001 and $15,000 on Sept. 9.
A week later, the Department of Housing and Urban Development awarded Palantir a contract with $10.4 million in initial obligations for AI-powered grant oversight and fraud detection.
On Sept. 29, the Department of Homeland Security awarded Palantir another $32.1 million software contract , bringing the two awards to roughly $42.5 million. That same day, CEO Alex Karp joined Trump, Musk, Huang and other technology executives at the White House for a meeting on artificial intelligence .
Trump's accounts also bought shares and debt in SpaceX in the weeks surrounding a major NASA contract award.
On Sept. 1, the accounts purchased between $100,001 and $250,000 in SpaceX debt carrying a 5.35% interest rate. Eight days later, they bought between $1,001 and $15,000 in shares of the major NASA and Pentagon contractor.
On Sept. 18, NASA announced a $946 million expansion of its SpaceX contract, adding three astronaut missions to the International Space Station and bringing the agreement's total value to $5.92 billion. The agency had signaled plans for additional missions in May.
Six days after the announcement, Trump's accounts bought another $15,001 to $50,000 in SpaceX shares on the same day Musk attended Trump's White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping . The filing does not show whether the purchase came before or after the dinner.
The trades followed an even larger SpaceX investment in August , when Trump's accounts bought between $1 million and $5 million in the company's debt just two days before he signed a policy aimed at expanding commercial space transportation.
Trump's accounts also continued buying Nvidia shares as Huang drew closer to the president — a relationship now under congressional scrutiny over Huang's ties to a woman suspected of spying for China.
The September filing shows four Nvidia purchases totaling between $152,004 and $380,000, including two on Sept. 2 worth as much as $350,000 combined.
The accounts also sold between $1,001 and $15,000 in Nvidia shares on Sept. 24, the day Huang also attended the state dinner with Xi.
The trades bring Trump's Nvidia transactions to at least 108 since his return to office in 2025, worth between $27.2 million and $97.9 million, extending a CNBC analysis published Monday .
The relationship between the president and Nvidia's then-CEO has drawn fresh scrutiny after The New York Times reported that intelligence officials warned Trump about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Trump has denied being briefed. Huang resigned Nov. 12 following revelations about his personal relationships.
The September filing also shows substantial trading beyond the three companies. The largest reported transaction was a Sept. 23 purchase of between $5 million and $25 million in Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF shares.
That same day, Trump's accounts sold between $1 million and $5 million each in Comcast , McDonald's , Home Depot and Fidelity National Information Services , along with between $500,001 and $1 million each in Nike and Constellation Brands .
On the buy side, Trump's accounts purchased between $250,001 and $500,000 in TJX shares on each of two consecutive days, Sept. 15 and 16. They also bought between $117,004 and $330,000 in Tesla shares across four transactions, along with smaller investments in CoreWeave , Intel , Microsoft and Apple .

articles.title_orig: UK to provide Ukraine with long-range drones as part of £260m package
articles.title_zh: UK to provide Ukraine with long-range drones as part of £260m package
articles.content_orig:
The UK will provide Ukraine with 1,000 long-range strike drones to target Russia beyond the front line, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced.
The drone support was announced at a meeting in Berlin of Ukraine's allies, the Coalition of the Willing, and is part of a new £260m package to boost its war defences this winter.
The government said the drones are able to fly up to 625 miles (1,000km) and carry heavier warheads, enabling Ukraine to target military production facilities.
The move is the latest sign of a growing British involvement in drone technology for Ukraine. The government said 80% of the package will be spent in the UK.
The Berlin talks came as US President Donald Trump is meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese Premier Xi Jinping.
Ahead of that meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in China, Trump said both he and Xi want to see an end to the Ukraine war.
In a statement released ahead of the latest meeting of the group of 36 countries committed to supporting Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire or peace agreement - the government said the UK is also building maritime, logistical and surveillance drones to help Ukraine's war effort.
Burnham, who co-chaired the meeting, had said the UK must do everything it can to make sure Ukraine can defend itself from Russian attacks throughout the winter.
Speaking at a press conference after the talks, Burnham said the mood of the coalition is "more determined than ever to stay the course" in support of Ukraine.
He welcomed the presence of US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff at the meeting and described Russia as "perhaps the biggest losers" of the conflict, as he referred to casualties they have suffered.
Burnham said: "This clearly has got to be a moment to move towards peace because of the US involvement that we've seen today and the progress clearly that is being made.
"Europe is ready to enter these negotiations, we are clear about what we will accept and what we won't accept, but we are also clear that we stand with Ukraine today, tomorrow, for as long as it takes, until this unjust war is over."
Before this latest support package was announced, government figures put the amount of support provided by the UK for Ukraine since Russia invaded the country in February 2022 at £35.5bn.
In recent days, Ukraine has struck oil refineries in southern Russia, and has repeatedly hit the Crimean Bridge - a significant logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.
Meanwhile, Russian forces have been focused on knocking out power in Ukraine before winter with attacks on critical infrastructure.
The UK is among a number of countries also supplying Ukraine with lightweight missiles which are being used to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.
Ukraine's strike rate is now close to 70%, more than double what it was just a couple of months ago, Downing Street said.
The UK also pledged further air defence support this week and sanctioned Russia's 10 major oil producers.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the government was delivering on a promise for more support for Ukraine at the Budget.
"Ukraine's frontline is the frontline for freedom and democracy, and we will stand with them for as long as it takes," he said.
Meanwhile, on Friday Burnham will head to Brussels for a UK-EU summit, where both sides hope to unveil new agreements on food, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime.
